options.text: two small nuclei join to build a larger nucleus
options.explanation: Fusion is the merging of light nuclei.

options.text: one big nucleus dividing into two smaller ones
options.explanation: That is fission, the opposite process.

options.text: a nucleus releases a gamma ray only
options.explanation: Gamma decay changes no nucleus at all.

options.text: a neutron turns into a proton
options.explanation: That is beta decay inside a nucleus.

questions.stem: Deuterium and tritium nuclei fuse together. What do they form?

options.explanation: Those are fission daughters of uranium.
Two hydrogen isotopes merge into helium, releasing energy.
Fission fuels are heavy nuclei; fusion builds light ones up.
The nuclei join; they do not stay apart.

questions.stem: Where does nuclear fusion happen naturally?

options.explanation: Atmospheric conditions are far too cool for fusion.
Ores decay, they do not fuse.
Star cores are hot and dense enough for fusion to run by itself.
Reactors currently use fission; fusion reactors are still in development.

questions.stem: The three sources of nuclear energy are…

options.explanation: Burning and evaporation are chemical, not nuclear.
Combustion is chemical energy, not nuclear.
Photosynthesis stores light energy, not nuclear energy.
All three open the energy stored in nuclei.

questions.stem: Fusing 1 kg of hydrogen releases roughly the energy of burning…

options.explanation: The corpus equivalence for hydrogen fusion is about 10,000,000 kg of coal.
That underplays the yield by a factor of a thousand.
Fusion outshines coal by many orders of magnitude.
The stated factor is ten million, not one million.

questions.stem: Name the three sources of nuclear energy.
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclear fusion, nuclear fission and radioactive decay.

questions.stem: State what forms when deuterium and tritium fuse.
questions.modelAnswer: A helium nucleus forms, with a large release of energy.

questions.stem: Explain why stars can power themselves by fusion but Earth cannot rely on natural fusion.
questions.modelAnswer: Star cores reach temperatures and pressures far beyond anything found naturally on Earth, so hydrogen nuclei there collide hard enough to merge, while everyday Earth conditions stay far too cool and roomy for fusion to run by itself.

questions.stem: A fusion trial consumes 2 kg of hydrogen. Using the coal equivalence, how many kilograms of coal would release the same energy?
questions.modelAnswer: 1 kg of hydrogen fused matches about 10,000,000 kg of coal, so 2 kg matches 2 × 10,000,000 = 20,000,000 kg of coal.

questions.stem: Nuclear fission is best described as…

options.text: a nucleus releasing only gamma rays
options.explanation: Gamma emission leaves the nucleus unsplit.

options.text: one large nucleus splitting into two smaller nuclei
options.explanation: Fission divides a heavy parent into two daughters.

options.text: two small nuclei joining into one larger nucleus
options.explanation: That is fusion.

options.text: an atom losing an orbital electron
options.explanation: Electron loss is ionisation, not nuclear fission.

questions.stem: The fragments produced when a parent nucleus splits are called…

options.explanation: The established term is daughters.
Beta particles are emitted electrons, not fragments.
The split products carry the daughter name.
The parent is the nucleus that split, not the fragments.

questions.stem: Which machines generate electricity from fission today?

options.explanation: Fusion reactors are in development, not yet commercial.
Coal burns chemically; no nuclei split.
Solar panels convert light, not nuclear energy.
Controlled fission is the working reactor technology.

questions.stem: In fission, the large original nucleus is named the…

options.explanation: Parent is the established name for the splitting nucleus.
Daughters are the two fragments produced.
No such term exists in the topic.
The topic's word is parent.

questions.stem: Which statement about fission energy is correct?

options.explanation: Fission also generates electricity in power stations.

options.text: energy stored in the nucleus is released when it splits
options.explanation: The split frees nuclear energy, often as kinetic energy of the products.
Energy is released from a store, never conjured.

options.text: fission absorbs more energy than it gives back
options.explanation: Fission is a net energy release.

questions.modelAnswer: Nuclear fission is the splitting of one large nucleus into two smaller nuclei, with the release of energy.

questions.stem: State where fission is used to generate electricity.
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclear power stations use controlled fission to generate electricity.

questions.stem: Explain why fusion and fission both count as sources of nuclear energy.
questions.modelAnswer: Both reactions release the energy stored inside nuclei: fusion frees it when small nuclei merge, fission frees it when a large nucleus is split, so either route taps the same nuclear store.

questions.stem: An engineer describes 'one heavy nucleus dividing into two lighter nuclei, with energy out'. Name the process and the fragment nuclei.
questions.modelAnswer: The process is nuclear fission, and the two lighter product nuclei are the daughter nuclei of the parent.
